appraisal_events.evidence: Ce fut un long défilé, mais un défilé devant le baron seul... Aucune ne s'occupait de Mme Verdurin... Mme d'Arpajon me demanda... « Est-ce qu'il y a seulement jamais eu un M. Verdurin ? »... Cette politesse au mari seul était... le plus sanglant outrage pour l'épouse.
appraisal_events.explanation: The departing guests queue almost exclusively to thank and flatter Charlus as though he alone were host, entirely bypassing Mme Verdurin — mistaking another woman for her, doubting her husband's existence — while Charlus's own speech credits himself for the evening and then snubs her further by inviting only her husband elsewhere.

appraisal_events.evidence: Il est immonde, répondit-elle... Je sais qu'il a eu de sales histoires et que la police l'a à l'œil... Il paraît qu'il a fait de la prison... Il tient Charlus par des lettres qui sont quelque chose d'effrayant... Il mourra assassiné un jour ou l'autre, comme tous ses pareils d'ailleurs.
appraisal_events.explanation: Mme Verdurin unleashes an escalating, self-admittedly improvised string of slanders against Charlus — calling him vile, inventing a criminal record and a blackmail plot by Jupien — to enlist Brichot in separating him from Morel.

appraisal_events.evidence: la comtesse Molé n'était pas égale à l'extraordinaire réputation d'intelligence qu'on lui faisait, et qui donnait à penser à ces acteurs ou à ces romanciers médiocres qui... ont une situation de génies, soit à cause de la médiocrité de leurs confrères... soit à cause de la médiocrité du public.
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator states outright that Molé's celebrated reputation for intelligence exceeds her real merit, comparing her to mediocre performers mistaken for geniuses only because of the low standards around them.

appraisal_events.evidence: Je fus très étonné de voir, là, aussi aimable et flagorneur avec M. de Charlus qu'il était sec avec lui autrefois... M. d'Argencourt, cet homme si terrible pour l'espèce d'hommes dont était M. de Charlus... voulant à la fois la préserver et la distraire, ne le pouvait sans danger qu'en l'entourant d'hommes inoffensifs, à qui il faisait ainsi jouer le rôle de gardiens du sérail.
appraisal_events.explanation: A formerly hostile d'Argencourt now courts Charlus's company, a reversal the narrator immediately undercuts by revealing it is purely instrumental — Charlus and his like are being used as harmless guardians around d'Argencourt's mistress.

status_effects.explanation: The departing guests entirely bypass her as hostess — mistaking another woman for her, doubting her husband's existence — treating her as absent from her own salon.
Guests queue and linger almost exclusively to thank and flatter him, and he holds forth as though he alone were host, a vivid public display of commanding local position.
Mme Verdurin brands him 'immonde' and fabricates a criminal past and blackmail plot in order to destroy his standing with Brichot and pave the way for removing him from Morel's life.
The narrator notes her 'don d'improvisation' for malice, exposing the slanders as invented even as she postures as Morel's protector.
The narrator flatly deflates her vaunted reputation for intelligence as unearned, comparing her to mediocrities mistaken for geniuses.
A once openly hostile figure now seeks him out and flatters him, a visible if instrumentally motivated rise in his local reception, distinct from the dominance shown in E1.

ambiguities: The narrator calls Charlus's self-congratulatory speech in E1 a symptom of 'la démence de ceux que Jupiter veut perdre,' foreshadowing his coming downfall even as the scene itself stages him at the peak of local social command; the positive delta reflects that staged local reality rather than the foreshadowing.

Mme Verdurin's slanders against Charlus in E2 are explicitly marked by the narrator as invented, so the negative delta records the passage's local discrediting effect on Charlus's reputation with Brichot rather than any endorsed factual claim about him.
